parts.title: Enquiring about a summer camp
parts.context: A father asks about places at a summer camp for his son.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a father phoning a summer camp to ask about places for his son. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: Oakwood Summer Camp, Ms Walsh speaking.

script.speaker: wei
script.text: Hello. I'd like some information about your summer camps, please. They're for my son.

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: Of course. I'll take a few details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The camp is for the caller's son, so 'son' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: wei
script.text: Wei Zhang. That's Z-H-A-N-G.

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: Thank you, Mr Zhang. And your son's name?

script.speaker: wei
script.text: Leo. L-E-O.

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: How old is Leo?

script.speaker: wei
script.text: He's nine, but he'll be ten in August.

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: What does he enjoy doing?

script.speaker: wei
script.text: Football, mainly, and he loves painting. He's always drawing something.

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: Which week would suit you?

script.speaker: wei
script.text: The week beginning the fourteenth of July, if there's space.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: There is. We have three kinds of camp that week. The Adventure camp includes climbing, canoeing and archery, and it costs thirty-five pounds a day.

script.speaker: wei
script.text: That sounds exciting, but he's a bit nervous of water.

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: In that case, the Art camp might suit him better. The children do painting and puppet making, and at the end of the week, they put on a show. That's twenty-eight pounds a day.

script.speaker: wei
script.text: He'd like that. What about the third?

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: The Science camp, with experiments, and a trip to the museum on Wednesday. It's thirty pounds a day.

script.speaker: wei
script.text: I think the Art camp is best for Leo, but could he try football as well?

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: Yes, every afternoon, there's a free hour of sports on the field, whichever camp the children are in.

script.speaker: wei
script.text: Perfect. Is lunch included?

script.speaker: walsh
script.text: Yes, and a snack in the afternoon. Just tell us about any allergies. I'll send you the booking form.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A residential summer camp
parts.context: A director describes the week at a summer camp.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a camp director describing the programme of a week-long residential summer camp. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: Welcome, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information evening about our residential summer camp. I'm Alan Boyd, the camp director, and I'll start by telling you what the week looks like.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: The children arrive on Monday afternoon, and spend the first evening getting to know one another. On Tuesday, there's a treasure hunt across the whole site, in teams, which is a good way to make friends.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: On Wednesday evening, we go on a night hike, with torches, to a hill near the camp. The children love it, though some are a little scared at first, and the leaders stay close.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: Thursday is the swimming gala, at the lake, with races and games, and prizes for every team. Friday evening is the talent show, when the children sing, dance or perform magic tricks.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: And on Saturday, before everyone goes home, there's a campfire barbecue, where we hand out certificates. Parents are welcome to join us for that. There are no activities on Sunday, because the camp is closed.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: Some details you'll want to know. About eighty children come each week, in groups of ten, and each group has two leaders, one of whom is always a trained first-aider.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: Please don't let your children bring mobile phones. We have a phone that they can use in the evenings to call home, and it helps them to join in with the activities instead of looking at screens.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: Sleeping bags are provided, but many children like to bring their own, and a favourite soft toy is very welcome.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: It's quite common for a child to feel homesick, especially on the second night. If it happens, they talk to a counsellor, who is trained to help, and in nearly every case the child is happy again by the next morning.

script.speaker: boyd
script.text: To keep you informed, we post photographs on the camp website every day, so you can see what your child has been doing. Now, are there any questions?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: The ethics of self-driving cars
parts.context: Two philosophy students plan an essay.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two philosophy students, Naomi and Theo, discussing the ethics of self-driving cars. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Theo, shall we plan the essay on self-driving cars? I think we should begin with the arguments in favour.

script.speaker: theo
script.text: Yes. The strongest one is that they would cause fewer accidents, because most crashes are caused by human error, such as tiredness or distraction.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: And a second argument is that they could reduce traffic. If cars communicate with each other, they can travel closer together and avoid jams.

script.speaker: theo
script.text: Cheaper insurance is sometimes mentioned, but I don't think it's convincing. Nobody knows yet how insurance would work.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Now the main ethical problem. Who is responsible when a self-driving car causes an accident?

script.speaker: theo
script.text: That's the question the essay should focus on. I'd say the manufacturer, because it designed the software, but the owner might also be responsible if they didn't keep it updated.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: We could include the famous dilemma, where a car must choose between two harmful actions.

script.speaker: theo
script.text: It's interesting, but it's a rare situation, and Dr Hall said we should not spend more than a paragraph on it.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: What about privacy? These cars collect a huge amount of data about where people go.

script.speaker: theo
script.text: Yes, that deserves a section, because the data could be sold to advertisers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: How long is the essay supposed to be?

script.speaker: theo
script.text: Two thousand words, and we have until the end of the month.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: I suggest we divide it. You take the arguments in favour, and I take the ethical problems.

script.speaker: theo
script.text: Fine. Should we include interviews with drivers?

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: No, we don't have the time. I'd prefer to use published research, and a couple of news reports.

script.speaker: theo
script.text: Where should we look for the research? The library only has a few books.

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: The journals online are better. I'll send you the links tonight.

script.speaker: theo
script.text: Good. And when shall we meet to put it together?

script.speaker: naomi
script.text: Next Friday, in the library. Then we'll have a week to edit.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: desertification
parts.context: A lecture on the causes of desertification and some solutions.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about desertification. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about desertification, which is the process by which fertile land gradually turns into desert. It is one of the most serious environmental problems in the world, and it affects the lives of hundreds of millions of people.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Drylands, meaning the regions where rainfall is low, cover about forty percent of the Earth's land surface. They are home to about a billion people, many of whom depend on farming and herding animals.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: What causes desertification? Climate plays a part, especially long droughts, but human activity is usually the main cause. The first is overgrazing. When too many animals feed on the grass, the plants cannot recover, and the ground is left bare.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The second is the removal of trees. People cut down trees for firewood or to clear land, and without roots to hold it, the soil is exposed. Third, poor farming methods, such as growing the same crop year after year, exhaust the soil.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Once the plants have gone, the wind and rain remove the topsoil, the thin fertile layer on the surface. It takes hundreds of years to form, but it can be lost in a single storm, and once it has gone, the land may never recover.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: One of the worst affected regions is the Sahel, the broad belt of land on the southern edge of the Sahara in Africa. Droughts there in the nineteen seventies and eighties caused famine, and the desert has steadily advanced.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: But there are solutions. The Great Green Wall is a project to plant a belt of trees across Africa, from Senegal in the west to Djibouti in the east, and to restore the land along its path. Individual farmers can help, too, by building stone walls or terraces on slopes, which stop the rain washing away the soil, and by using drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots, and wastes very little.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The lesson is that, with care, damaged land can recover. Next week we'll look at the problem of water scarcity.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
